chapterTitle: Ansible Vault for Sensitive Data Management

screens.title: Ansible Vault for Sensitive Data Management
screens.narratorSegment: In automation, secrets like database passwords, A P I keys and private keys are unavoidable. This lesson shows you how to keep those items encrypted at rest with Ansible Vault so they are unreadable without the vault password. You will learn the core commands to create, edit, view, encrypt, decrypt, and embed secrets; how Ansible decrypts data in memory during runs; and why secure vault password handling is the single most important operational control. For example, you'll see how a group_vars file encrypted with Vault can be used by a playbook at runtime without exposing secrets in your repository. We'll also cover vault identifiers for separate environments, and practical steps such as using a vault password file with strict permission bits. By the end you will understand not only the commands but the tradeoffs: interactive prompting versus automated password files, the risk of committing password files, and how to avoid printing secrets to logs. Keep your vault passwords safe and remember: losing a vault password means losing the data irrecoverably. Consider this lesson the security checklist you follow before you ever add a credential to source control.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive data so automation can use secrets securely without storing them in plain text.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Ansible Vault Overview
Ansible Vault for Sensitive Data
Protect credentials and secrets used by your automation workflows.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Why Vault matters

Secrets committed to Git can be leaked. Vault encrypts files so stored credentials remain unreadable without the vault password.

How it works

Ansible uses symmetric encryption: the same password encrypts and decrypts. At runtime it decrypts in memory and does not write plain text to disk.

Quick commands
ansible-vault create
ansible-vault encrypt
ansible-vault decrypt
In this lesson

You will learn commands, integration patterns, password handling options, vault IDs, and common mistakes to avoid when managing secrets in automation.

Visual
Vault file
group_vars/all/vault.yml encrypted at rest
Password file
Use a protected vault password file with strict permissions for automation
Runtime
Ansible decrypts in memory during playbook runs and discards plain text afterward
Explore key topics
Commands: create, edit, view, encrypt, decrypt, encrypt_string
Password handling: prompt, password file, env, ansible.cfg
Best practices: no hardcoding, secure permissions, avoid printing secrets

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify when to use Ansible Vault, perform essential Vault operations, integrate encrypted variables into playbooks, and implement secure password handling for automated runs. First, you will understand the threat model: why plain-text secrets in repositories are a liability and how symmetric encryption mitigates that risk. Second, you will practice creating and editing vault files, viewing encrypted content safely, and encrypting plain files or single strings for direct embedding. Third, you will learn how to have Ansible decrypt data at runtime using a prompt, a password file, an environment variable, or an ansible configuration, and the tradeoffs of each method. Finally, you will be guided through Vault IDs to manage different environment keys and a short checklist of best practices such as restrictive file permissions, avoiding debug prints of secrets, and not committing password files. Each objective is a practical competency you can verify by running the included hands-on activity.

screens.title: Why Ansible Vault?
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Vault exists to solve a simple but critical problem: you must never store secrets in plain text inside automation repositories. If credentials, A P I keys, or private keys are committed to version control, anyone with repository access or access to logs can misuse them. Vault addresses this by encrypting sensitive data at rest so that stored files are unreadable without the vault password. The encryption in Ansible Vault is symmetric, which means the same secret is used to encrypt and to decrypt. That design makes the password the single key to the kingdom: secure its storage and access. Consider the workflow: you encrypt a file, commit the ciphertext to source control, and then provide the vault password only at runtime or via a protected mechanism. Ansible will decrypt into memory while the playbook runs and then discard the plaintext, reducing the window of exposure. A common misconception is that Vault hides secrets during execution; Vault protects data at rest but you still must avoid printing secrets to logs or output. Use no_log on tasks that touch secrets and ensure files containing passwords have restrictive file permissions. As a learner, remember: Vault reduces one major risk vector, but correct operational choices around password management and logging are equally important.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive data at rest using symmetric encryption so playbooks can use secrets securely without storing plaintext.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Why Ansible Vault?
Problem and model

Storing secrets in plain text is a high-risk practice. Vault encrypts files so only those with the vault password can decrypt them.

Symmetric encryption

Vault uses a single password for both encrypting and decrypting. Protect this password carefully; losing it means losing access to encrypted values.

Key Takeaway

Vault secures secrets at rest; operational practice secures the password and runtime handling.

Common misconception

Vault does not prevent secrets from being printed at runtime. Use no_log and avoid debug prints of sensitive variables.

Analogy

Think of Vault as a locked safe stored in a shared room. The safe holds secrets encrypted. The key is the vault password. You can share the safe's contents only with someone who has the key; losing the key or leaving it on the desk is where breaches happen.

Practical example
ansible-vault create group_vars/all/vault.yml
# create opens your editor to save encrypted variables
Why it matters

Proper use of Vault prevents accidental exposure in source control and limits secret access to controlled runtime contexts.

screens.title: Core Vault Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Mastering a few commands gives you immediate control over secrets. Start with ansible-vault create followed by a filename to open an editor and save encrypted variables. Use ansible-vault edit to update an existing encrypted file; it decrypts temporarily for editing and re-encrypts on save. If you need to inspect contents without editing, ansible-vault view shows the decrypted file after prompting for the password. To secure an accidentally committed plain-text file use ansible-vault encrypt filename, which replaces the file with ciphertext. Only use ansible-vault decrypt when you intentionally need a plaintext copy, and do so with extreme caution because that file may now be exposed. Keep in mind that ansible-vault encrypt is destructive to the plain file content and replaces it with encrypted data, so ensure backups or version control practices before converting. Practice these steps until the flow feels natural: create, edit, view, encrypt, and decrypt only when necessary. One common slip is forgetting to provide the vault password at runtime — plan your decryption method in advance. Finally, remember that encrypting at the file or string level gives you flexibility: large credential stores can be separate files, and small secrets can be embedded using the encrypt_string command covered next.

keyIdea.title: Commands
keyIdea.text: Use create, edit, view, encrypt, and decrypt carefully to manage the lifecycle of encrypted files.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Core Vault Commands
Command sequence
1. ansible-vault create <file> — create and save a new encrypted file via editor.
2. ansible-vault edit <file> — open an encrypted file for safe edits.
3. ansible-vault view <file> — decrypt temporarily to inspect contents.
4. ansible-vault encrypt <file> — convert plain text to encrypted file.
5. ansible-vault decrypt <file> — revert to plaintext (use cautiously).
Tip: Always back up before decrypting and avoid decrypting on shared filesystems.
Example session
ansible-vault create group_vars/all/vault.yml
# prompts for a new password, opens editor for you to add variables
Supporting notes
  • Editing re-encrypts on save, so you don't manually handle ciphertext.
  • Use view when you must confirm values without accidental edits.
  • Encrypt will replace the original file with its encrypted form.

screens.title: Encrypting Individual Strings
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes you only need to store a single secret inside a vars file or a playbook rather than a whole encrypted file. For that use case, ansible-vault provides encrypt_string which takes a plain string and returns a YAML-compatible vaulted block you can paste into a variables file. The command prompts for a password and prints the encrypted variable labeled with the name you provide. This is handy for quick one-off secrets or for adding a vaulted variable in a code review without touching an entire file. A practical example is producing an encrypted A P I key and placing it under vars in a role. One misconception is treating the output as human-readable; the output is ciphertext and must be copied in full including the variable name and the vault marker. Also remember that the resulting vaulted string is decrypted the same way as vaulted files — Ansible requires the vault password to use that variable at runtime. Use encrypt_string for small secrets, and prefer separate vault files for larger or grouped credentials to keep organization clear. Encrypting Individual Strings means encrypt_string creates a yaml-compatible encrypted variable block suitable for embedding in vars or playbooks.. In practical terms, use encrypt_string to embed a single vaulted variable in yaml. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Encrypt string
keyIdea.text: encrypt_string creates a YAML-compatible encrypted variable block suitable for embedding in vars or playbooks.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Encrypt a single string
Use case

When a single secret must be embedded in a vars file or playbook, encrypt_string produces the necessary vaulted YAML block.

Command pattern
ansible-vault encrypt_string 'mysecretvalue' --name 'my_secret_variable'
Output notes

The tool prints a YAML block that looks like a variable assignment followed by a vault marker and the ciphertext. Copy the whole block into your vars file exactly as shown.

Example use

Embed an encrypted API key in role defaults or group_vars without creating a separate file if it is truly a single secret.

Misuse check

Avoid overusing encrypt_string for many secrets; prefer organized vault files for maintainability.

screens.title: Using Vaulted Variables in Playbooks
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating vaulted variables into playbooks is straightforward when you follow conventions. Ansible automatically looks for group_vars and host_vars directories, so placing an encrypted file named vault. yml under group_vars/all makes its variables available to all hosts. For files outside that convention, use vars_files or include_vars to explicitly bring them into scope. During playbook execution Ansible attempts to decrypt any vaulted file it encounters, provided it has access to the vault password or password file you supply. A concrete example is a playbook that references db_password and api_key coming from group_vars/all/vault. yml; the tasks can use those variables in templates or module arguments. Remember to avoid printing secrets in debug tasks: printing decrypted variables to console or logs undermines Vault. Use no_log on tasks that handle sensitive values. Also ensure that files created on target hosts that contain secrets have restrictive permissions like mode 0600. In practice, keep your vaulted variables organized by environment or role so that secrets are easy to find and rotate when needed. Using Vaulted Variables in Playbooks means place vault.yml in group_vars or include encrypted files with vars_files so ansible decrypts them at runtime when the vault password is provided.. In practical terms, how ansible finds and decrypts vaulted data during runs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Integration
keyIdea.text: Place vault.yml in group_vars or include encrypted files with vars_files so Ansible decrypts them at runtime when the vault password is provided.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Using Vaulted Variables
Automatic discovery and explicit includes

Ansible checks group_vars and host_vars automatically. For other locations, use vars_files or include_vars to load vaulted files into the play scope.

Sample playbook snippet
- name: Deploy application with sensitive credentials
  hosts: webservers
  vars_files:
    - group_vars/all/vault.yml
  tasks:
    - name: Configure database connection
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: templates/db_config.j2
        dest: /etc/app/db_config.conf
      vars:
        db_user: "{{ db_username }}"
        db_pass: "{{ db_password }}"
Notes and checklist
  • Ensure Ansible has the vault password at runtime; otherwise decryption fails.
  • Do not use debug to print secrets; instead use no_log or safe verification messages.
  • Keep vault files organized per environment or role for easier rotation.
Key takeaway

Vaulted variables plug into playbooks like normal variables, but require a vault password to decrypt at runtime.

screens.title: Vault Password Delivery Options
screens.narratorSegment: Providing the vault password is required whenever Ansible needs to decrypt a vaulted item. There are four common delivery options, each with tradeoffs. First, the interactive prompt using --ask-vault-pass is secure for manual runs because it never stores the password on disk, but it does not suit automation. Second, a vault password file given via --vault-password-file is the usual choice for automated systems; the file must contain only the password and be secured with restrictive permissions, for example 0600. Third, you can place the password file path in an environment variable so that orchestration tools inject it at runtime, which centralizes configuration but still requires careful permission handling. Fourth, setting vault_password_file in ansible. cfg makes decryption automatic for runs under that configuration, which is convenient but requires preventing that configuration file from being exposed or committed. One misconception is treating a password file as less risky; it must be protected as strongly as any secret. Always gitignore password files and apply strict filesystem permissions. Decide based on whether you run interactively or in CI/CD: use the prompt for ad hoc runs and a protected password file for automation.

keyIdea.title: Password options
keyIdea.text: Choose a password delivery method based on security needs: prompt for manual runs, protected files for automation, and strict permissions always.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Vault Password Delivery
Delivery options
--ask-vault-pass — interactive prompt; secure but not automated.
--vault-password-file <file> — file containing only the password; ideal for automation with strict permissions.
Environment variable — pass the password file path via env var for orchestration; still secure the file.
ansible.cfg — set vault_password_file for automatic use from that configuration; convenient but handle the config securely.
Security checklist
  • Never commit password files to Git; add them to .gitignore.
  • Set tight file permissions, e.g., chmod 0600 on vault password files.
  • Prefer password prompt for interactive sessions to avoid disk persistence.
Operational note

Automated CI/CD pipelines typically use a vault password file placed in a secure runner workspace; ensure the file is ephemeral and permission-restricted.

screens.title: Vault IDs for Multiple Environments
screens.narratorSegment: Vault IDs let you use multiple vault passwords in one project. This is useful when environments require separate keys: for example, a development vault and a production vault. You can encrypt files with a vault ID and either prompt for the password or supply a different password file per ID at runtime. The typical pattern is to annotate encrypted files or commands with an identifier, for example encrypting a dev secrets file with a dev vault ID and a prod file with a prod vault ID. When running a playbook you provide the corresponding vault IDs and password sources so Ansible knows which key to try for each encrypted block. A common practical setup: ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id dev@prompt dev_secrets. yml and ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id prod@/path/to/prod_pass. txt prod_secrets. yml. During execution you pass both vault IDs and supply the necessary passwords. This approach reduces the blast radius of a compromised password because keys are scoped to environments, but it does add operational overhead for managing multiple password files and rotation procedures. Vault IDs for Multiple Environments means vault ids let you encrypt different files with different passwords and supply multiple passwords at runtime for environment separation.. In practical terms, use vault ids to manage different vault passwords across dev, staging, and prod. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vault IDs
keyIdea.text: Vault IDs let you encrypt different files with different passwords and supply multiple passwords at runtime for environment separation.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.5 › Vault IDs
Why use Vault IDs?

Separate secrets for dev, staging and production reduce risk. Vault IDs assign an identifier to each password so multiple keys can coexist in a project.

Example commands
ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id dev@prompt dev_secrets.yml
ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id prod@/path/to/prod_pass.txt prod_secrets.yml
Runtime example

When running a playbook you can pass multiple vault IDs so Ansible can try the right password for each encrypted file.

Key takeaway

Vault IDs enable environment separation at the cost of managing multiple passwords and rotation policies.

screens.title: Secure Password and File Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Managing the vault password securely is as important as using Vault itself. Treat any file that contains the vault password as a secret: it should contain only the password, be listed in. gitignore, and have restrictive permissions such as chmod 0600. Consider creating a temporary vault password file on the runner at build time and removing it after the playbook completes. Never commit vault_pass. txt to source control. For team environments, use shared secret stores or an operations process that distributes password files securely rather than emailing them. When creating or copying files that contain secrets onto target hosts ensure the destination file uses restrictive permissions, for example mode 0600, so only the intended user can read it. Also avoid using debug tasks to print secret values. If you must verify a value during testing, log only non-sensitive confirmation messages. Remember that encrypting everything is not always practical; encrypt only what is sensitive to reduce operational friction and keep secrets discoverable for rotation and auditing. Secure Password and File Handling means protect vault password files with strict permissions, gitignore them, avoid printing secrets, and encrypt only truly sensitive data.. In practical terms, practical guidelines for managing vault passwords and secured files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Managing the vault password securely is as important as using Vault itself. Also avoid using debug tasks to print secret values. If you must verify a value during testing, log only non-sensitive confirmation messages. Remember that encrypting everything is not always practical; encrypt only what is sensitive to reduce operational friction and keep secrets discoverable for rotation and auditing. screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes when teams adopt Vault. First, hardcoding passwords directly in playbooks or inventory is the most common and damaging error — avoid it entirely. Second, losing the vault password is irreversible; encrypted data cannot be recovered without it, so store passwords securely and consider a documented recovery plan. Third, committing the vault password file to Git or leaving it with permissive file modes defeats Vault; always. gitignore and restrict permissions. Fourth, over-encrypting everything can create unnecessary operational burden — encrypt only truly sensitive variables. Finally, exposing decrypted data through debug output or pipeline logs is a frequent operational slip; tasks that process secrets should use no_log: true to prevent output. A practical defensive habit is to scan playbooks for debug tasks before running in production and to use file permission checks on any file that will hold secret content on the target host. These small practices prevent the majority of real-world leaks and keep Vault effective in protecting secrets. fullNarratorScript:
In automation, secrets like database passwords, A P I keys and private keys are unavoidable. This lesson shows you how to keep those items encrypted at rest with Ansible Vault so they are unreadable without the vault password. You will learn the core commands to create, edit, view, encrypt, decrypt, and embed secrets; how Ansible decrypts data in memory during runs; and why secure vault password handling is the single most important operational control. For example, you'll see how a group_vars file encrypted with Vault can be used by a playbook at runtime without exposing secrets in your repository. We'll also cover vault identifiers for separate environments, and practical steps such as using a vault password file with strict permission bits. By the end you will understand not only the commands but the tradeoffs: interactive prompting versus automated password files, the risk of committing password files, and how to avoid printing secrets to logs. Keep your vault passwords safe and remember: losing a vault password means losing the data irrecoverably. Consider this lesson the security checklist you follow before you ever add a credential to source control.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify when to use Ansible Vault, perform essential Vault operations, integrate encrypted variables into playbooks, and implement secure password handling for automated runs. First, you will understand the threat model: why plain-text secrets in repositories are a liability and how symmetric encryption mitigates that risk. Second, you will practice creating and editing vault files, viewing encrypted content safely, and encrypting plain files or single strings for direct embedding. Third, you will learn how to have Ansible decrypt data at runtime using a prompt, a password file, an environment variable, or an ansible configuration, and the tradeoffs of each method. Finally, you will be guided through Vault IDs to manage different environment keys and a short checklist of best practices such as restrictive file permissions, avoiding debug prints of secrets, and not committing password files. Each objective is a practical competency you can verify by running the included hands-on activity.

This second objectives slide gives a concrete checklist you can follow during practice and assessment. You will create an encrypted file with ansible-vault create and save strong secrets inside. You will open and edit that file with ansible-vault edit and use ansible-vault view to confirm encrypted content without exposing it in repository history. You will convert an accidental plain-text credentials file to an encrypted one with ansible-vault encrypt and understand when decrypting is acceptable. You will use encrypt_string to produce a YAML-ready vaulted string for single variables. Finally, you will verify runtime decryption using ask-prompt, a secure vault password file with limited permissions, environment variables or an ansible. cfg setting, and learn how to combine multiple vault IDs for separate environments. Each item is demonstrable in a lab environment and maps to the hands-on activity in this chapter.

Ansible Vault exists to solve a simple but critical problem: you must never store secrets in plain text inside automation repositories. If credentials, A P I keys, or private keys are committed to version control, anyone with repository access or access to logs can misuse them. Vault addresses this by encrypting sensitive data at rest so that stored files are unreadable without the vault password. The encryption in Ansible Vault is symmetric, which means the same secret is used to encrypt and to decrypt. That design makes the password the single key to the kingdom: secure its storage and access. Consider the workflow: you encrypt a file, commit the ciphertext to source control, and then provide the vault password only at runtime or via a protected mechanism. Ansible will decrypt into memory while the playbook runs and then discard the plaintext, reducing the window of exposure. A common misconception is that Vault hides secrets during execution; Vault protects data at rest but you still must avoid printing secrets to logs or output. Use no_log on tasks that touch secrets and ensure files containing passwords have restrictive file permissions. As a learner, remember: Vault reduces one major risk vector, but correct operational choices around password management and logging are equally important.

Mastering a few commands gives you immediate control over secrets. Start with ansible-vault create followed by a filename to open an editor and save encrypted variables. Use ansible-vault edit to update an existing encrypted file; it decrypts temporarily for editing and re-encrypts on save. If you need to inspect contents without editing, ansible-vault view shows the decrypted file after prompting for the password. To secure an accidentally committed plain-text file use ansible-vault encrypt filename, which replaces the file with ciphertext. Only use ansible-vault decrypt when you intentionally need a plaintext copy, and do so with extreme caution because that file may now be exposed. Keep in mind that ansible-vault encrypt is destructive to the plain file content and replaces it with encrypted data, so ensure backups or version control practices before converting. Practice these steps until the flow feels natural: create, edit, view, encrypt, and decrypt only when necessary. One common slip is forgetting to provide the vault password at runtime — plan your decryption method in advance. Finally, remember that encrypting at the file or string level gives you flexibility: large credential stores can be separate files, and small secrets can be embedded using the encrypt_string command covered next.

Sometimes you only need to store a single secret inside a vars file or a playbook rather than a whole encrypted file. For that use case, ansible-vault provides encrypt_string which takes a plain string and returns a YAML-compatible vaulted block you can paste into a variables file. The command prompts for a password and prints the encrypted variable labeled with the name you provide. This is handy for quick one-off secrets or for adding a vaulted variable in a code review without touching an entire file. A practical example is producing an encrypted A P I key and placing it under vars in a role. One misconception is treating the output as human-readable; the output is ciphertext and must be copied in full including the variable name and the vault marker. Also remember that the resulting vaulted string is decrypted the same way as vaulted files — Ansible requires the vault password to use that variable at runtime. Use encrypt_string for small secrets, and prefer separate vault files for larger or grouped credentials to keep organization clear. Encrypting Individual Strings means encrypt_string creates a yaml-compatible encrypted variable block suitable for embedding in vars or playbooks.. In practical terms, use encrypt_string to embed a single vaulted variable in yaml. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integrating vaulted variables into playbooks is straightforward when you follow conventions. Ansible automatically looks for group_vars and host_vars directories, so placing an encrypted file named vault. yml under group_vars/all makes its variables available to all hosts. For files outside that convention, use vars_files or include_vars to explicitly bring them into scope. During playbook execution Ansible attempts to decrypt any vaulted file it encounters, provided it has access to the vault password or password file you supply. A concrete example is a playbook that references db_password and api_key coming from group_vars/all/vault. yml; the tasks can use those variables in templates or module arguments. Remember to avoid printing secrets in debug tasks: printing decrypted variables to console or logs undermines Vault. Use no_log on tasks that handle sensitive values. Also ensure that files created on target hosts that contain secrets have restrictive permissions like mode 0600. In practice, keep your vaulted variables organized by environment or role so that secrets are easy to find and rotate when needed. Using Vaulted Variables in Playbooks means place vault.yml in group_vars or include encrypted files with vars_files so ansible decrypts them at runtime when the vault password is provided.. In practical terms, how ansible finds and decrypts vaulted data during runs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Providing the vault password is required whenever Ansible needs to decrypt a vaulted item. There are four common delivery options, each with tradeoffs. First, the interactive prompt using --ask-vault-pass is secure for manual runs because it never stores the password on disk, but it does not suit automation. Second, a vault password file given via --vault-password-file is the usual choice for automated systems; the file must contain only the password and be secured with restrictive permissions, for example 0600. Vault IDs let you use multiple vault passwords in one project. This is useful when environments require separate keys: for example, a development vault and a production vault. You can encrypt files with a vault ID and either prompt for the password or supply a different password file per ID at runtime. The typical pattern is to annotate encrypted files or commands with an identifier, for example encrypting a dev secrets file with a dev vault ID and a prod file with a prod vault ID. When running a playbook you provide the corresponding vault IDs and password sources so Ansible knows which key to try for each encrypted block. A common practical setup: ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id dev@prompt dev_secrets. yml and ansible-vault encrypt --vault-id prod@/path/to/prod_pass. txt prod_secrets. yml. During execution you pass both vault IDs and supply the necessary passwords. This approach reduces the blast radius of a compromised password because keys are scoped to environments, but it does add operational overhead for managing multiple password files and rotation procedures. Managing the vault password securely is as important as using Vault itself. Treat any file that contains the vault password as a secret: it should contain only the password, be listed in. gitignore, and have restrictive permissions such as chmod 0600. Consider creating a temporary vault password file on the runner at build time and removing it after the playbook completes. Never commit vault_pass. txt to source control. For team environments, use shared secret stores or an operations process that distributes password files securely rather than emailing them. When creating or copying files that contain secrets onto target hosts ensure the destination file uses restrictive permissions, for example mode 0600, so only the intended user can read it. Also avoid using debug tasks to print secret values. If you must verify a value during testing, log only non-sensitive confirmation messages. Remember that encrypting everything is not always practical; encrypt only what is sensitive to reduce operational friction and keep secrets discoverable for rotation and auditing. There are recurring mistakes when teams adopt Vault. First, hardcoding passwords directly in playbooks or inventory is the most common and damaging error — avoid it entirely. Second, losing the vault password is irreversible; encrypted data cannot be recovered without it, so store passwords securely and consider a documented recovery plan. Third, committing the vault password file to Git or leaving it with permissive file modes defeats Vault; always. gitignore and restrict permissions. Fourth, over-encrypting everything can create unnecessary operational burden — encrypt only truly sensitive variables. Finally, exposing decrypted data through debug output or pipeline logs is a frequent operational slip; tasks that process secrets should use no_log: true to prevent output. A practical defensive habit is to scan playbooks for debug tasks before running in production and to use file permission checks on any file that will hold secret content on the target host. These small practices prevent the majority of real-world leaks and keep Vault effective in protecting secrets.
